I.
CONTEXT

The Ituri province is located in the Northeast of the Democratic Republic of Congo and shares a long border with Uganda and South Sudan.
For more than two decades, it has been confronted with a chronic humanitarian crisis linked to armed conflicts and recurrent population displacement.
It has an estimated population of over 8 million inhabitants, including more than one million internally displaced persons.

In September 2018, this province was affected by an Ebola virus disease epidemic that was raging in the neighboring North-Kivu province.

The health area of Mongbwalu is one of the 36 health areas in the Ituri province.
Considered as the starting point of the epidemic, it is located in the Djugu territory where several armed groups operate.
It is located 70 km from Bunia, the provincial capital of Ituri, with frequent population movements towards Uganda.
This locality has the particularity of having several construction sites that attract populations from other territories of the province and neighboring provinces.

1. Epidemic History

On May 5, 2026, social media reported an outbreak of deaths from unknown causes with nearly 50 deaths already recorded in the Mongbwalu health area.
After confirmation of this alert, the Chief Medical Officer of the Mongbwalu health area shared the preliminary investigation report on May 9, 2026.
On May 11, 2026, provincial health authorities organized an emergency meeting and decided to deploy rapid intervention teams to Mongbwalu and Rwampara, which had reported suspected deaths of viral hemorrhagic fever among patients admitted to the Rwampara Evangelical Medical Center, originating from Mongbwalu.

The investigations carried out on May 12, 2026, simultaneously in the health areas of Mongbwalu and Rwampara by the Rapid Intervention Teams of the Provincial Health Division (DPS) of Ituri made it possible to note that most of the suspected patients or deaths had fever, headaches, vomiting, and intense physical asthenia.
Deaths occurred 2 to 3 days after the onset of the illness with hematemesis, epistaxis, or blackish vomiting.
During investigations in the Rwampara health area, 20 samples were collected from suspected cases or deaths.
The majority of the individuals sampled came from the Mongbwalu health area.
Preliminary tests performed at the Bunia Laboratory were all negative for Ebola Zaire, dengue, Rotavirus, Cholera, Malaria, Yersinia pestis, mpox, and COVID-19.
These samples were sent to the National Institute of Biomedical Research (INRB) in Kinshasa for additional examinations.

On May 14, 2026, 13 cases out of these 20 samples were tested, and 8 tested positive for non-Zaire Ebola virus disease at INRB Kinshasa.
On May 15, 2026, sequencing of the positive samples identified the Bundibugyo strain, which allowed the Minister of Public Health, Hygiene and Social Welfare (MSHPS) to officially declare the 17th epidemic of Ebola virus disease.

Event classified as EVD (Ebola Virus Disease) species Bundibugyo.
| | May 15, 2026 | INRB Kinshasa confirms the Ebola virus (non-Zaire species).

HIGHLIGHTS

20 New confirmed cases as of May 18, 2026, including 18 in Ituri province and 2 in North-Kivu province.
As of May 18, 2026, a cumulative total of 33 confirmed cases, including 30 confirmed cases in Ituri and 3 in North-Kivu.
Two provinces affected: Ituri (4 HS: Bunia, Nyankunde, Mongbwalu, and Rwampara) and North-Kivu (3 HS: Katwa, Goma, and Butembo).
Livestock farmers at the TSERE farm in the Rwampara HS were sensitized on the non-consumption of meat from 5 pigs that died from an unspecified disease, and two showed hemorrhagic signs.
Result: The 5 dead pigs were denatured and buried;

IV. CHALLENGES

- Difficulty of mobility for teams for investigation at the DPS and HS levels.
- Difficulty of dispatching samples from Mongbwalu to the provincial laboratory in Bunia.
- Insufficiency of collection kits.
- Insufficiency of Protection Kits and surveillance tools.

V.
RECOMMENDATIONS * Strengthen intervention teams in the affected HS.
* Make available transportation means (mobility) to field teams.
* Fill the GAP in collection kits.
* Continue contact listing and start contact follow-up in all HS.
* Develop a mapping of population mobility in the affected health zones.
* Strengthen epidemiological surveillance and community-based surveillance.
* Train healthcare providers in epidemiological surveillance, community-based surveillance, and laboratory.
